history.title: Name What You Gave Up

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Choices use limited resources. This week you identify trade-offs and the value of the next-best alternative, central ideas in economics.

1. Read **Everything Has a Cost**.
2. Learn the words in **Choice Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Every Choice, Two Columns** chart open.
4. Trace **Why Choosing Is Unavoidable** before the quiz.
5. Sort the cards in **Scarce or Just Expensive?**
6. Take **Choice Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Second Best**.
8. Read **Money Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Decide: The Community Centre Hour**.

Your job this week: catch yourself making one real choice and name what you gave up. ⚖️

Picture panels: A limited shared resource; Feasible uses and choice; Trade-offs and opportunity cost; Past and additional costs. Pictures support interpretation of the editable lesson text; they are not standalone evidence or answer keys. Numerical records and named practice stories are fictional. Read each sort in its stated context. Educator review is pending.

Use the sort’s explicit time, place and recovery assumptions. Classify the named resource or past cost, not every aspect of the situation. Free access is not the same as unlimited supply everywhere.

history.title: Everything Has a Cost
history.data:
## Everything Has a Cost

You have one free hour. Suppose you can spend it on one of three mutually exclusive plans: see friends, work on a project, or rest. Choosing one prevents those same minutes from being used for another plan.

**Scarcity** means available resources cannot satisfy all the competing wants for them. It concerns time, money, materials, space and attention, not just rare or expensive objects. Whether a resource is scarce for a particular activity depends on what is available, where and when it is available, and how much is wanted. A free price does not guarantee unlimited availability.

A **choice** selects among feasible alternatives. A **trade-off** describes giving up one benefit or use to obtain another. Some choices allow combinations; our one-hour example rules them out so the comparison is clear.

**Opportunity cost** is the value of the next-best feasible alternative forgone. If you choose rest and seeing friends is your next-best option, the cost is the benefit you would have received from seeing friends during that hour. Do not add every lower-ranked option. If an alternative is a feasible combination of activities, evaluate that whole alternative rather than insisting it must be a single named activity.

Suppose a fictional town has a fixed budget and only two feasible, mutually exclusive proposals: a road or a library. If it chooses the road, the forgone library benefit is the opportunity cost. A real town may have many alternatives; you cannot assume the runner-up without examining them.

A **benefit** is an expected gain. Compare future benefits and costs using stated assumptions, including effects that are hard to express in money. Different people may rank options differently.

A **sunk cost** is a past cost that cannot be recovered. Suppose a film ticket cannot be refunded, resold or transferred. The purchase money is gone whichever activity you choose now. That past payment alone should not justify attending a film you no longer want to see. The remaining time, travel cost and expected experience still matter. If a refund or resale is possible, that recoverable value is relevant.

Past training time cannot be recovered, but the skills you gained can affect future choices. Likewise, already-owned equipment may have future use or resale value. Do not confuse a sunk purchase cost with an asset's remaining value.

A **marginal** decision compares an additional benefit with an additional cost: is one more hour of practice worth what that hour displaces? An **incentive** changes a choice's expected benefit or cost. It can influence choices without forcing everyone to respond the same way.

In the community-room task, one room is available from four to five and four groups want the entire slot. Rank the feasible uses, explain your criteria, identify the next-best forgone benefit, and distinguish unrecoverable past spending from consequences that remain ahead.

The sort's scenarios are fictional and include explicit assumptions. “Available for this use” does not mean the resource is unlimited everywhere. Classify the highlighted resource or past expenditure in its stated context.

history.title: Money Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Is anything actually free? 🤔
data.answer: A zero price does not mean zero opportunity cost. Attending a free event uses time that might have another valued use; specify the relevant alternative rather than assuming every free object is scarce in the same way.

data.question: If I enjoy both options equally, is the cost zero?
data.answer: No. If the alternatives are equally valued, the forgone value can still be substantial even though you are indifferent between them. Opportunity cost is not the difference between their values or a measure of regret.

data.question: Does this mean money decisions are the only real ones? 💸
data.answer: No. Time and space choices also involve trade-offs. Paying for a faster option may be reasonable under a person’s circumstances, but the price alone does not prove a choice is best.

data.question: Why do people fall for sunk costs so often?
data.answer: Past investments can make people reluctant to stop. Separate unrecoverable past expenditure from remaining costs, benefits, information and recoverable value.

data.question: Is scarcity the same as poverty? ⚖️
data.answer: No. Scarcity is the general constraint of limited resources relative to wants. Poverty concerns inadequate resources for meeting important needs; its consequences are not the same as every ordinary trade-off.

data.question: Can a government just make more of something?
data.answer: Additional production can expand available options, but it uses resources. Examine which resources have alternative uses and their forgone value rather than assuming every worker or material is already assigned to another project.

data.title: The Community Centre Hour
data.instructions: Four groups want the same hour in the same room. Recommend one, name the opportunity cost precisely, and defend it to the group that loses.
data.fitReason: D2.Eco.2 asks students to evaluate alternatives in terms of benefits and costs. Forcing one recommendation from four claims on a genuinely scarce resource makes opportunity cost something they have to name rather than define.

brief.context: The community centre has one room free on Tuesdays from four to five. Four groups have asked for it: a homework club, a seniors' exercise class, a youth band rehearsal, and a food-bank sorting session. Only one can have it. This is a classroom simulation. State assumptions about attendance, access, noise, staffing and benefits; the brief gives no verified rankings. No publication or real booking is implied.
brief.audience: All four groups, who will each be told the decision and the reason
brief.drivingQuestion: Which group should get the hour, what exactly is the opportunity cost of that decision, and can you justify it to the group that came second?
brief.seedDirection: Rank all four before you decide. You cannot name an opportunity cost without knowing which one came second.
lockedLessonFacts: Scarcity means available resources cannot satisfy all competing wants.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best feasible alternative forgone.
Only unrecoverable past costs are sunk.
Equipment may retain future use or resale value.
openQuestions: How do you compare benefits that are not measured in the same units?
Does it matter how many people each group serves, or who they are?
Would your answer change if one group had already bought equipment for that room?
stakeholders: The four groups competing for the hour
The centre staff who must explain the decision
People served by the group that loses
criteria: All four options are ranked, not just the winner named
Name the next-best feasible use and the value of its forgone benefit, explaining the ranking
At least one benefit that is hard to measure is acknowledged rather than ignored
The sunk-cost question is answered explicitly
At least four glossary words used correctly
constraints: One hour, one room, one group
A decision is required; no splitting the hour
Every claim needs a stated reason
brief.deliverable: A panel decision: the ranked list of four, the recommendation, the opportunity cost named precisely, and a short paragraph addressed to the second-place group explaining the reasoning.

parallelExample.context: Invented example: a panel initially favors an exercise group because it already bought mats.
parallelExample.move: The panel separates the unrecoverable part of the past purchase from the mats’ remaining use and any resale value. It compares future benefits and costs of all four options; this review may or may not change its recommendation.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: The example avoids treating an asset as worthless just because money was spent in the past.
